title: Editorial
author: Faruk Abdulkadir Waziri (Editor-in-Chief)
quote: "Engineering does not end at the blueprint; its true value lies in transforming ideas into practical solutions that improve lives."  — Faruk Abdulkadir Waziri Editor-in-Chief
rawContent:
# Editorial

> “Engineering does not end at the blueprint; its true value lies in transforming ideas into practical solutions that improve lives.”
>
> — Faruk Abdulkadir Waziri  
> Editor-in-Chief

There is a peculiar contradiction in the way we sometimes approach engineering. We spend years learning how to make things work, yet the world around us keeps presenting reasons why so many things do not. We understand the principles behind electricity generation, but millions still have to negotiate their daily lives around its availability. We study energy conversion, efficiency, protection, and control, while businesses continue to spend a considerable part of their earnings keeping their operations alive. We learn to design systems, but the challenge of making those systems accessible, reliable, and sustainable remains very much before us.

It is a contradiction worth thinking about. More importantly, it is a reminder of why engineering matters.

The value of engineering cannot be measured solely by the complexity of the systems we design, the sophistication of the technologies we adopt, or the number of equations we can solve. Its significance is found in what these things make possible. A reliable power supply means more than electricity reaching a consumer; it means a business that can operate with fewer interruptions, a hospital that can depend on its equipment, a student who can study without constantly negotiating with darkness, and an industry that can produce without the burden of an unreliable energy supply. Behind what may appear to be ordinary conveniences are problems that demand serious thought, sound engineering, and practical solutions.

It is from this understanding that we present this edition of the NIEEE Final-Year Magazine, themed *BEYOND THE BLUEPRINT: Engineering Solutions to Nigeria’s Electrical, Energy, and Technological Challenges.*

The theme is deliberate. A blueprint represents thought, calculation, and intention. It is where an idea begins to take shape, where possibilities are examined and a proposed solution is given structure. But engineering cannot end there. A design must contend with materials, operating conditions, economic realities, safety requirements, human needs, and the many uncertainties that accompany implementation. What appears convincing on paper must still prove itself in practice. To go beyond the blueprint, therefore, is to concern ourselves not only with what can be designed, but with what can actually work, who it will serve, and whether it can be sustained.

For Nigeria, these questions are particularly important. Our energy challenges are neither unfamiliar nor difficult to identify. They are visible in the instability of electricity supply, the cost of alternative power, the limitations of existing infrastructure, and the uneven access to modern energy services. They extend into agriculture, manufacturing, healthcare, education, and virtually every sector that depends on reliable electricity. Yet, alongside these difficulties are opportunities for better engineering, more deliberate planning, local innovation, and the thoughtful application of emerging technologies.

The contributions in this edition approach these concerns from different perspectives. Our writers examine the reliability of electricity distribution networks, the possibilities of renewable energy and battery storage, and the role of mini-grids in extending electricity access. Other articles explore the application of artificial intelligence to power system monitoring, the potential of blockchain in electricity trading, and the place of renewable energy in agricultural development. We also consider something less confined to a particular technology but equally important: the habit of thinking like an engineer and applying that discipline to the problems encountered in everyday life.

![[../images/faruk_abdulkadir_waziri.jpg]]

These subjects may differ in their technical approaches and the possibilities they explore, but they share a common question: how can the knowledge of our discipline be made useful beyond the walls of the university?

It is a question worth asking, especially at a time when technological advancement is often mistaken for progress. The introduction of a new technology does not automatically constitute a solution. Artificial intelligence, blockchain, renewable energy, and other emerging fields offer considerable possibilities, but their usefulness depends on more than their novelty. They must be assessed against actual needs, technical limitations, affordability, safety, and the conditions under which they are expected to operate. Sometimes, what a problem requires is not a sophisticated invention but a better understanding of its cause. At other times, it demands the courage to question established methods and consider alternatives.

We believe that engineering education should cultivate both dispositions. It should produce graduates who understand the theories behind their discipline, but who are equally prepared to confront the realities those theories must address. It should encourage curiosity without sacrificing rigour, innovation without neglecting safety, and ambition without losing sight of practical limitations. Above all, it should remind us that engineering is ultimately a human undertaking. The systems we design exist within communities, serve people, consume resources, and carry consequences beyond the calculations from which they emerge.

This publication is one modest contribution to that conversation. It does not claim to have exhausted the questions raised by our theme, nor do the articles presented here pretend to offer final answers to challenges that have persisted for decades. Rather, we hope to encourage inquiry, make room for ideas, and demonstrate that students of Electrical and Electronics Engineering are capable of engaging with the realities of their discipline beyond examinations, laboratory exercises, and academic requirements.

I am particularly pleased with the opportunity this magazine provides for our students to research, write, question, and share their perspectives. There is value in learning a subject, but there is another kind of learning that comes from attempting to explain it, examining its relevance, and defending an idea before others. I hope this experience encourages our contributors to continue developing that habit long after this edition has been published.

To our contributors, thank you for trusting us with your ideas and giving this edition its substance. To the editorial committee, whose time and effort have gone into reviewing, refining, and bringing these contributions together, I offer my sincere appreciation. I also acknowledge the support and guidance of our lecturers, the Department, and everyone who has contributed in one way or another to the realisation of this publication.

To our readers, I invite you to approach these pages with curiosity. Question the arguments, consider the possibilities, and perhaps look differently at some of the challenges we have grown accustomed to discussing. If this edition succeeds in doing anything, I hope it reminds us that the problems around us are not merely things to complain about or become accustomed to. They are also things to investigate, understand, and work towards solving.

We may begin with a blueprint, but we cannot afford to end there.

**Faruk Abdulkadir Waziri**  
Chief Editor  
NIEEE Final-Year Magazine  
Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering  
Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University, Bauchi

title: Message from the Dean
author: Prof. Ya'u S. Haruna (Dean, Faculty of Engineering & Engineering Technology)
rawContent:
# Message from the Dean

MESSAGE FROM THE DEAN
”LEADERSHIP BUILT ON EXPERIENCE AND CLEAR
GOALS”
— Prof. Y. S. Haruna

With experience as Head of the Department of Electrical and
Electronics Engineering and later as Deputy Dean, the
interviewee brings a department-level and faculty-wide
perspective to the challenges facing engineering education. In
this conversation, he reflects on the department’s reputation,
crowded classrooms and laboratories, the need to turn
research into practical solutions, and the importance of setting
clear professional goals.
“Always set a target. Monitor your progress and see whether
you are on the right track.”
1. Having served as Head of Department and now as Dean,
how has the move from departmental to faculty leadership
changed your understanding of the challenges facing
engineering education?
I served as Head of Department for nine years and later as
Deputy Dean for four years. Those roles gave me experience of
the challenges at both departmental and faculty levels. The
department is where many of the day-to-day issues begin, and
as Head of Department I handled a range of responsibilities,
including examinations, records, and student matters. That
experience has helped me understand the work that reaches
the Dean’s office. Leadership also requires managing the needs
and expectations of both students and academic staff.
2. What would you consider the department’s most
significant achievement, and which areas still need greater
attention?
One of the department’s strongest achievements has been its
reputation for producing graduates with a sound
understanding of engineering theory and practice. In the past,
graduates were highly regarded by employers, and some
secured employment opportunities soon after industrial
training. The department has built a name for itself nationally.
However, large class sizes create serious difficulties. Classes can
have at least 150 students, while dedicated teaching spaces are
limited. Laboratories designed for much smaller groups also
struggle to accommodate the current student population.
3. What practical research is being carried out to address
Nigeria’s electricity and energy challenges?
Our postgraduate students and researchers work on problems
related to improving electricity supply. Some projects focus on
reducing technical losses in power systems, while others
examine how thermal and hydroelectric generation can be
balanced to reduce operating costs. Research also explores
ways of adding to existing hydroelectric capacity, including
investigating photovoltaic installations on water. These are
examples of how university research can be directed towards

the country’s energy needs.
4. Why do many university research projects fail to become
practical solutions, and what needs to change?
This is a challenge across Nigerian universities. In some
countries, industries bring specific problems to universities,
and researchers develop solutions that the industries then
adopt. Here, many projects end up on library shelves, often
serving mainly as a requirement for obtaining a qualification.
Greater collaboration is needed between government,
universities, and industry. Government can help by
encouraging companies to present their problems to
universities, supporting research, and creating conditions for
successful projects to be implemented.
5. What contribution do you hope students and colleagues
will remember from your leadership?
I have tried to remain accessible to students and to address
their concerns when they bring them forward. One area I
focused on was reducing delays in postgraduate completion.
Some students spent many years on their master’s degrees
after completing coursework without moving their projects
forward. I encouraged them to choose topics, consult their
supervisors, and present their research synopses. This helped
more students make progress and complete their programmes
without unnecessary delays. I also encouraged timely
postgraduate completion and hoped other departments would
adopt similar practices.
6. What advice would you give graduating students as they
begin their professional journeys?
Do not underestimate the value of your final-year project. Take
part in every stage of its design and construction, even when
someone is helping you. A project can develop into a useful
skill, a product, or even a source of livelihood. Learn the
principles behind what you build and keep developing that
knowledge. I would also advise graduates to set clear targets.
Decide what you want to achieve, monitor your progress, and
adjust your approach when necessary. I used this method in
planning my own academic and professional development,
including research publications, postgraduate qualifications,
and promotion. Finally, learn from people with more
experience and stay focused on the goals you have set.
7. What early-career advice has remained valuable to you?
Life is a journey, and learning from those ahead of you can help
you prepare your own path. Set a target and keep checking
whether you are moving in the right direction. If you are falling
behind, work out what needs to change; if you are progressing
well, look for ways to improve further. Having a plan helped me
decide what I wanted to achieve over the following years and
work steadily towards it.

# From the HOD’s Desk

FROM THE HOD'S DESK
”LEADERSHIP, LEARNING & ENGINEER’S MINDSET”
— Prof. A. L. Amoo

In this conversation, the department’s leader discusses the T
strengths of its academic community and the practical f
challenges facing electrical engineering education. The o
interview also considers curriculum relevance, laboratory c
resources, professional development, and the importance s
of treating student projects as opportunities to build real o

The department is still using the Benchmark Minimum c

Some topics and examples, particularly in c

Practical laboratory work is an important part of the c

The department also benefits from a legacy of engineering

outdated, while other items cannot be used because
components or accessories are missing. The number of
students has also grown beyond what some facilities were
originally designed to accommodate. Alumni support has
helped: the department received equipment and
accessories valued at approximately ₦7 million during the
period mentioned in the interview. The university
management is also working with departments on

4. Beyond academic performance, what qualities and
competencies should every graduating student
possess?
Graduates should be able to communicate, socialise, and

balanced graduate should be able to work with others and
contribute responsibly to society.
5. What advice do you have for the graduating class,

Take your project seriously and make an effort to

construction and testing—even when someone is helping
you. Do not treat a project as just a requirement to
complete before graduation. Practical projects can become
the foundation for future employment, entrepreneurship,
or further innovation. Engineers have developed useful
products and tools from ideas that may initially appear
small. Mastering one area of electrical engineering and
continuing to develop that skill can open doors later in your
career.
6. What lesson from your own experience would you
like to share with graduates beginning their
professional journeys?
Hold firmly to your values and beliefs, respect people of
different backgrounds, and be a patriotic and honest citizen.
The interviewee emphasised that honesty, responsibility,
and listening to one’s parents are important principles to

title: From Reactive to Predictive: How Artificial Intelligence Can Make Nigeria’s Power Grid More Reliable
author: Afolabi Wasiu Opeyemi | 500L
quote: "Could smarter use of operating data help Nigerian electricity utilities identify problems earlier, forecast demand more accurately and plan maintenance before equipment fails?"
rawContent:
# From Reactive to Predictive: How Artificial Intelligence Can Make Nigeria’s Power Grid More Reliable

**Author:** Afolabi Wasiu Opeyemi | 500L

> “Could smarter use of operating data help Nigerian electricity utilities identify problems earlier, forecast demand more accurately and plan maintenance before equipment fails?”

## A smarter approach to maintenance

Nigeria’s electricity challenges are not limited to generation and transmission capacity. The way existing networks are monitored, maintained and operated also affects the quality of supply. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, offers tools that can help utilities make better use of information already produced by power-system equipment.

## Turning measurements into early warnings

Corrective maintenance begins after equipment has failed, while preventive maintenance is usually performed at planned intervals. Predictive maintenance uses condition data to estimate when an inspection or intervention may be needed. For example, an AI model could examine transformer temperature, load current, voltage and operating history to identify unusual patterns that deserve an engineer’s attention. A prediction is not proof that a failure will occur: inspection and established protection procedures remain essential.

## Forecasting demand and detecting faults

AI-supported monitoring can combine measurements from sensors, smart meters and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems. These may include voltage, current, frequency, temperature and equipment status. Machine-learning models can use historical demand and influencing factors such as weather, time and consumer activity to forecast electricity loads. The article cites a study of the Abuja Municipal Area Council distribution network in which an artificial neural network produced a lower reported mean absolute percentage error than the multiple linear regression model used for comparison. AI may also help flag abnormal equipment conditions, although incomplete fault records and rare failure events can make reliable prediction difficult.

## What Nigeria needs to make it work

Wider adoption faces practical barriers: incomplete historical records, limited sensor coverage, inconsistent data collection, cybersecurity risks, implementation costs and shortages of specialised personnel. Models can also produce false alarms or miss unfamiliar faults. A sensible starting point is a pilot project at selected transformers or substations. Engineers should test models on independent data, compare them with established methods and monitor performance as operating conditions change. Universities, distribution companies and technology organisations can work together to develop local datasets and skills.

## THE TAKEAWAY

AI should strengthen—not replace—engineering judgement and conventional protection. Used carefully, it can help utilities move from reacting to failures towards better-informed forecasting, diagnosis and maintenance.

## REFERENCES

- T. D. Makanju, T. Shongwe and O. J. Famoriji, “Machine Learning Approaches for Power System Parameters Prediction: A Systematic Review,” IEEE Access, vol. 12, pp. 66646–66679, 2024. doi: 10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3397676.
- E. C. Ashigwuike et al., “Medium Term Electrical Load Forecast of Abuja Municipal Area Council Using Artificial Neural Network Method,” Nigerian Journal of Technology, vol. 39, no. 3, pp. 860–870, 2020. doi: 10.4314/njt.v39i3.28.
- O. Olasupo, T. R. Ayodele and A. S. O. Ogunjuyigbe, “A Survey of Electricity Load Forecasting Approaches with Insights from the Nigerian Power Sector,” Nigerian Journal of Technology, vol. 45, no. 3, pp. 534–551, 2026. doi: 10.67358/njt.2026.5898.

title: Beyond the Substation: Improving the Reliability of Nigeria’s Electricity Distribution Networks
author: Hussaini Adamu Hardawa | 500L
quote: "Reliable electricity depends not only on generating and transmitting power, but also on the condition of the distribution lines, transformers and protection systems that deliver it to consumers."
rawContent:
# Beyond the Substation: Improving the Reliability of Nigeria’s Electricity Distribution Networks

**Author:** Hussaini Adamu Hardawa | 500L

> “Reliable electricity depends not only on generating and transmitting power, but also on the condition of the distribution lines, transformers and protection systems that deliver it to consumers.”

## The last stage of electricity delivery matters

Nigeria’s electricity supply challenge does not end when power reaches a transmission substation. Distribution networks carry electricity from transmission interface points through distribution substations, feeders and transformers to homes, schools, hospitals and businesses. Weak conductors or connections, deteriorated poles, damaged insulators, overloaded equipment and poorly coordinated protection can interrupt supply even when power is available upstream.

## Understanding the causes of outages

Rain, wind, lightning, vegetation and contaminated or damaged insulators can contribute to faults on overhead lines. Loose joints, inadequate clearances, ageing equipment and poor maintenance can create additional risks. Hardawa draws on his industrial training at the Yola 330/132/33 kV transmission substations and observations of interruptions in Bauchi to highlight the gap between bulk-power infrastructure and the service consumers experience. He is careful to note that rainfall occurring before an outage does not, by itself, prove that rain caused the fault. Each interruption should be investigated using fault records and technical inspection.

## Engineering standards and preventive maintenance

The article stresses that reliability depends on suitable materials, correct equipment ratings, secure joints, sound earthing, adequate clearances and properly selected and coordinated protective devices. Aluminium conductors, which are widely used because they are lighter and generally less expensive than copper, are not inherently unreliable; problems arise when conductors are incorrectly selected or sized, connections are poorly made, or maintenance is neglected. Maintenance teams should inspect vulnerable sections, manage vegetation, test protection systems and keep records of fault causes and restoration times. Work on electrical infrastructure must be undertaken by trained and authorised personnel using approved safety procedures.

## Accountability and practical priorities

The Electricity Act 2023 provides a framework for state-level electricity markets and regulation, while responsibilities across generation, transmission, distribution and regulation remain distinct. The presence of power at a transmission substation cannot guarantee that every feeder can deliver it reliably. Hardawa recommends technical audits of feeders and equipment; transparent reporting of interruption frequency, duration and restoration time; stronger training and engineering supervision; and investment linked to measurable improvements in reliability, safety and customer service. Better coordination among transmission operators, distribution companies, regulators and government agencies is also needed.

## THE TAKEAWAY

A dependable electricity supply requires more than generation capacity. Safe distribution equipment, competent personnel, preventive maintenance, sustained investment and transparent accountability are essential to getting power from the substation to the consumer.

## REFERENCES

- Federal Republic of Nigeria, Electricity Act, 2023.
- Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), regulations and reports on distribution service quality.

title: Powering the Plough: Integrating Renewable Energy into Nigeria’s Agricultural Value Chain
author: Sarkes Lawehmat Silas | 300L
quote: "Reliable renewable electricity can do more than light rural homes: it can help farmers irrigate fields, preserve produce and reduce the cost of agricultural operations."
rawContent:
# Powering the Plough: Integrating Renewable Energy into Nigeria’s Agricultural Value Chain

**Author:** Sarkes Lawehmat Silas | 300L

> “Reliable renewable electricity can do more than light rural homes: it can help farmers irrigate fields, preserve produce and reduce the cost of agricultural operations.”

## The energy challenge on farms

Agriculture remains important to Nigeria’s economy, but many farming communities have limited access to reliable and affordable energy. Farmers often depend on rainfall or expensive petrol- and diesel-powered generators for irrigation, processing and storage. Fuel costs can make dry-season farming less profitable, while the lack of dependable cold storage contributes to the spoilage of tomatoes, vegetables, dairy products and other perishable goods. Farmers may have to sell quickly, sometimes at reduced prices.

## Solar power for irrigation and storage

Solar-powered irrigation systems use photovoltaic panels to supply electricity to surface or submersible pumps drawing water from suitable sources such as boreholes and rivers. Correct system sizing is essential, and motor controllers or variable frequency drives can help regulate pump operation. Where water storage is available, farmers can pump during sunny periods and store water for later use. Solar-powered cold rooms and rural storage hubs can also help preserve produce. Battery storage or thermal storage can maintain suitable temperatures when solar generation is low; thermal storage may use phase-change materials that absorb and release heat.

## Making productive use of land and farm waste

The article also explores agrivoltaics, where solar panels and crop production share the same land. Panel positioning and shading must be managed carefully because crops differ in their sunlight requirements. Agricultural residues and livestock manure can provide another energy resource. Through anaerobic digestion, these materials can produce biogas for cooking and some thermal processing activities, while helping manage organic waste.

## From promising ideas to workable projects

High initial costs for panels, pumps, batteries and cold-storage equipment can prevent smallholder farmers from adopting these systems. A shortage of trained technicians and limited access to spare parts can also leave equipment out of service. Farmers and developers may struggle to obtain affordable finance. The article therefore recommends targeted green loans and grants, training through engineering departments and vocational institutes, and public-private partnerships involving government, energy developers, farmers and cooperatives. Local maintenance support should be planned from the beginning of each project.

## THE TAKEAWAY

Renewable energy can strengthen the agricultural value chain by lowering operating costs, supporting dry-season irrigation and reducing post-harvest losses. To deliver these benefits, projects must be affordable, properly designed and supported by local skills and maintenance.

## REFERENCES

- International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), *Renewable Energy for Agriculture: Insights and Policies*, 2023.
- Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), *The Impact of Post-Harvest Losses on Food Security in Sub-Saharan Africa*, 2022.
- Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP), *Decentralized Solar Solutions for Rural Productivity and Economic Growth*, 2024.

title: Beyond the Grid: How Renewable Energy and Mini-Grids Can Electrify Rural Nigeria
author: Umar Ibrahim (Anchau) | 500L
quote: "For communities far from existing electricity infrastructure, well-designed renewable-energy mini-grids can offer a practical route to reliable local power."
rawContent:
# Beyond the Grid: How Renewable Energy and Mini-Grids Can Electrify Rural Nigeria

**Author:** Umar Ibrahim (Anchau) | 500L

> “For communities far from existing electricity infrastructure, well-designed renewable-energy mini-grids can offer a practical route to reliable local power.”

## Taking electricity closer to communities

Extending the national grid to every remote settlement can be expensive and technically difficult. Renewable-energy mini-grids provide another option for communities that are costly or challenging to connect. A mini-grid is a local network that generates and distributes electricity to homes, businesses and public facilities. It may operate independently or connect to the national grid where the technical and regulatory conditions allow.

## How a solar mini-grid works

A typical solar photovoltaic (PV) mini-grid with battery storage includes solar panels, power-conversion or charge-control equipment, a battery energy storage system, an inverter, protection devices and a local distribution network. During the day, the panels generate electricity for consumers and use surplus energy to charge the batteries. At night or when sunlight is insufficient, stored energy is delivered through the inverter to supply AC loads. Such systems can support lighting, refrigeration, water pumping, schools, healthcare centres and small businesses.

## The challenges behind the technology

The equipment requires substantial upfront investment, and batteries degrade over time and need eventual replacement. Poor system sizing, inadequate protection and limited technical expertise can shorten equipment life or cause unreliable service. Tariffs must also cover operation and future replacement costs without becoming unaffordable for low-income households. Before installation, developers need to understand daily energy use, peak demand, seasonal requirements, available solar resources and likely future growth.

## Designing for long-term success

The article recommends careful technical and economic assessments before equipment is selected. Battery storage and intelligent controls can help balance generation and demand, while smart meters, sensors and communication systems can allow operators to monitor voltage, current, battery condition and faults remotely. Local technicians should be trained in installation, troubleshooting, electrical safety and maintenance. Financing arrangements and compliance with applicable Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission requirements are also important. Finally, mini-grids should support productive uses such as irrigation, grain milling, refrigeration, workshops and small-scale manufacturing. These activities can strengthen local incomes and improve the financial sustainability of the system.

## THE TAKEAWAY

Mini-grids are not simply a matter of installing solar panels. Their long-term value depends on sound design, affordable finance, effective regulation, trained local technicians, preventive maintenance and active community participation.

## REFERENCES

- World Bank, *Expanding Nigeria’s Mini Grid Market*, 2025.
- International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), *Quality Infrastructure for Smart Mini-Grids*, Abu Dhabi, 2020.
- Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), *Mini Grid Regulations*, 2026.

title: Interview — Turning University Research into Local Solutions
rawContent:
# Interview — Turning University Research into Local Solutions

Engr. Ali Adamu — Dep. Director, CIS Directorate
Engineer Ali Adamu on industrial studies, research funding, and
building Nigerian capacity
“We are doing research based on our needs. If our university research
were fully utilised, many of our local problems could have been solved
by now.”
1. Could you briefly introduce yourself?
My name is Engineer Ali Adamu, and I am the Deputy Director of
the Centre for Industrial Studies (CIS).
2. Could you tell us about the Centre for Industrial Studies,
its main objectives, and its role in the university?
The Centre for Industrial Studies focuses on teaching and
carrying out industrial activities. It serves not only engineering
students but also students from other parts of the university,
including areas such as environmental and vocational education.
The centre provides practical training and supports design and
construction activities. It also undertakes postgraduate research
and development and works with professional bodies and
organisations on training activities, including the Nigerian
Institute of Welding, PTDF, ITF, and other partners.
3. University research often produces promising ideas that
never reach practical application. What do you think causes
this gap?
A major obstacle is inadequate funding. Research projects may
be completed and left unused while waiting for government
support. Research and development need regular funding, even
if the amounts are modest, because projects often require
continued work and refinement before they are ready for use.
We should not expect locally developed solutions to match
established foreign products immediately. Other countries have
improved their products gradually through ongoing research.
Our research is designed around our own needs, and sustained
investment could help it solve local problems.
4. How can the gap between university research and local
industries or communities be reduced?
Universities can develop designs, carry out simulations, and
demonstrate that a proposed solution works. Industry can then
help turn that research into a practical product. However,
Nigerian industries face their own financial and operational
challenges, which can make it difficult for them to fund
development and production. Better support and cooperation
between universities, government, and industry are needed to
help promising research move beyond the design stage.
5. What practical steps can universities take to strengthen
local research, innovation, and manufacturing?
We need to develop our own products and support their use. A
locally made product may not match an imported product at the
first attempt, but continued improvement can make it better
over time. If people and organisations are willing to patronise
local products, that support can encourage improvements in
design and construction and reduce dependence on imported
solutions.

6. How should researchers balance performance,
affordability, maintenance, and the availability of local
materials?
Government has an important role in creating a stable
economy and conditions that support local production. The
availability and price of materials affect whether a locally
made product can compete with an imported one.
Supporting domestic processing and manufacturing,
including the effective operation of rolling mills, could help
reduce material costs. Lower production costs would make
locally developed products more affordable to customers.
7. Are there opportunities for Electrical and Electronics
Engineering students at ATBU to participate in research,
industrial training, or innovation at CIS?
Yes. Research is increasingly interdisciplinary. Projects can
involve electrical and mechanical engineering, automation,
materials, chemical and petroleum engineering, civil
engineering, and other fields. For example, work involving
mineral resources may require materials testing, while
casting and construction may involve other engineering
disciplines. Electrical and Electronics Engineering students
can contribute to research and development at the centre
because many modern systems combine several areas of
engineering.
8. If students bring forward a promising solution to a
problem in their community, what would help it become
a practical, usable solution?
The project should address a real need and be useful to the
people who will use it. Students should consider whether
their proposed solution fits the local environment rather
than developing a project only to meet an academic
requirement. Nigeria has challenges involving power supply,
electronics, and electrical services. Students should explore
solutions that are practical, affordable, and easier to
maintain locally, reducing unnecessary dependence on
imported products. I would be willing to help where I can.
Engr. Ali Adamu

title: Interview — From Lab Reports to Real-World Skills
rawContent:
# Interview — From Lab Reports to Real-World Skills

Engr. Bashir Muhammad — Asst. Chief Lab Tech.
Engineer Bashir Muhammad on laboratory challenges, hands-
on learning, and preparing students for practice
“We are not here in the lab just to get grades and go. We
should be thinking further.”
1. How would you describe the current state of the
department’s laboratories in terms of equipment,
functionality, and support for practical training?
The department has six laboratories, and I currently oversee the
Control Engineering Laboratory while also taking care of the
Machines Laboratory following the retirement of the staff
member previously responsible for it. The laboratories face
equipment challenges. Some equipment is functional, some is
faulty, and some needs upgrading. The department has engaged
postgraduate students to help repair faulty equipment because
the university’s equipment and maintenance centre has not been
very active. Some equipment also requires compatible or
licensed software. For example, the magnetic levitation
equipment needs a suitable version of MATLAB. Although many
experiments can still be conducted, some equipment is decades
old. It teaches important first principles, but the laboratories
also need updating to reflect modern engineering practice. The
department keeps equipment inventories and provides status
reports when requested by management.
2. Should students be assigned projects that involve
repairing laboratory equipment rather than relying on
others to complete new projects for them?
Yes. I welcome the idea of assigning practical repair tasks to
students. Postgraduate students have already been given
challenging work, including repairs involving robotic arms,
magnetic levitation equipment, and LabVIEW processing units.
Undergraduate students could also be assigned tasks
appropriate to their level, such as repairing faulty AC or DC
power supplies and other smaller devices in the Machines
Laboratory. Tasks should be designed according to the student’s
level—undergraduate, master’s, or PhD—so the work is useful
and achievable.
3. Why do students sometimes understand theory but
struggle to implement or test what they have learned?
One problem is that some students treat practical classes mainly
as an exercise in submitting laboratory reports. A student may
submit a report without personally taking part in the
experiment, and sometimes the report becomes the main focus
for both students and staff. Practical classes must be taken
seriously, even when they carry only one credit unit. Students
should think beyond grades and consider the work they may do
after graduation—in power generation, transmission,
distribution, telecommunications, or other technical fields.
Employers will expect practical competence, including the ability
to use equipment safely. Laboratory training should help
students build the skills and confidence to work independently
or establish services such as solar installation, maintenance, or
consultancy.

4. Do students get enough hands-on time with
laboratory equipment?
Students should be able to connect circuits, take readings,
and record results themselves under the supervision of
laboratory technologists. If staff do all the connections and
measurements while students only watch, the experience
becomes too similar to classroom theory. However, many
laboratory modules are available in very limited quantities,
sometimes only one unit. This means students must be
allowed to practise while staff supervise closely to prevent
damage. Demonstration can come first, followed by
supervised student practice.
5. What practical skills should every Electrical and
Electronics Engineering student have before
graduation?
Students should gain practical experience related to the
department’s different areas, including power systems,
electrical machines, electronics, control, and
communications. Each course should include one or more
suitable experiments, provided the necessary equipment is
available. Where equipment is unavailable or faulty,
simulation software can be used as an alternative. Examples
mentioned include Livewire, Multisim, MATLAB, and
LabVIEW. Students should have an opportunity to perform
an experiment either with physical equipment or through an
appropriate simulation.
6. If you could change one thing about how students use
the department laboratories, what would it be?
I would encourage students to enter the laboratory with the
intention of learning, not merely submitting reports. Even
learning one basic skill—such as measuring AC or DC voltage
with a multimeter or checking a cable’s continuity—is
valuable. Gaining a real practical skill is better than
submitting many reports without understanding or learning
from the experiments.
Engr. Bashir Muhammad

![[../images/interview_bashir.jpg]]

---

title: Interview — Engineering Is More Than Passing Exams
rawContent:
# Interview — Engineering Is More Than Passing Exams

Meet Engr. A. I. Dalyop — Faculty Officer
A conversation on practical skills, innovation, and professional
character…
“Engineering training is all about developing the cognitive domain of
the student. It’s not about memorisation. You apply your understanding
to solve real problems.”
1. From your experience teaching in the department, what do students
most often misunderstand about electrical and electronics
engineering?
I would not necessarily say that students get the profession wrong.
Students come to the university to be guided, but they should also have an
ambition and some interest in the field. That interest may come from seeing
a parent or family friend work as an engineer, or from being fascinated by
how technology works or how devices are repaired.
What I have noticed over the years is that many students arrive without a
clear understanding of what engineering involves or of the foundational
subjects they will need. Mathematics and physics are particularly
important because electrical engineering relies heavily on them. A student
who comes in with a weak background in these subjects may struggle
unless they recognise the gap early and work hard to address it.
This points to a need for better guidance and counselling at secondary-
school level. Some students choose a course because their friends or
relatives are studying it, rather than because they understand it or have a
genuine interest in it. Interest matters in career development; when
students are interested and properly guided, learning becomes easier.
I have also observed this while screening new students for the department.
Sometimes a student's results look impressive, but when you ask basic
questions, the student struggles to respond. On the other hand, students
who can explain what they know and answer questions thoughtfully are
encouraging to see. It raises concerns about the declining standard of
preparation at the secondary-school level and the extent to which some
students rely on assistance to pass examinations.
2. What distinguishes a student who understands engineering
principles from one who has simply learned how to pass
examinations?
Engineering education should develop the student's ability to think deeply,
examine a problem, and visualise a possible solution. It is not simply about
memorising information. Understanding is important, and some
memorisation may be necessary, but the real test is whether a student can
apply that understanding to solve a problem in a new situation.
For example, if I teach a student how to solve a problem involving a
rectangular shape, I may then present a similar problem involving a
triangle. I want the student to think about what changes, what remains the
same, and how the shape affects the material or the solution. The student
should be able to explain and defend the approach they choose.
Engineering keeps evolving. Structures and technologies change, and
communication has moved from basic voice and text to images and video
transmitted wirelessly. An engineer cannot depend on being taught every
new development in a classroom. A strong foundation should enable them
to update their knowledge, adapt, and continue learning.
When a student has only memorised answers, a question presented in a
different way can become a problem. But when the student understands
the concepts, they can reason through the challenge, work with a team, and
consider the consequences of different solutions. That is what engineering
training should produce: people who can apply what they know to real
problems.
3. How can Nigerian engineers develop solutions that are technically
sound, affordable, maintainable, and suited to local conditions?
This requires cooperation among several stakeholders: engineers,
government, industry, academia, and the wider community. Government
has an important role in providing funding and an enabling environment,
while industries should communicate the challenges they need engineers
to solve. Universities can then connect their ideas and research to those
practical needs.
For example, if inadequate electricity is limiting small-scale industries in
Bauchi State, stakeholders could work together to examine ways of
improving supply. One possible approach might involve solar generation to

supplement the national grid. The point is to start with a real loca
problem and bring the relevant expertise and resources together t
address it.
Universities have ideas and student projects, but many remain at th
prototype stage because there is no clear path to further development
Technology-incubation centres should help promising ideas grow
connect inventors with support, and move projects closer to practica
use. However, those structures need to function effectively.
Our laboratories also need appropriate, modern equipment. Student
should be able to see how what they learn in class applies to rea
industrial processes. For instance, when teaching converters and
industrial drives, suitable laboratory modules and instruments can
help students observe waveforms and understand how the system
operate. If equipment is outdated or inadequate, students los
opportunities for practical learning.
Nigerian engineers are capable. We see professionals of Nigerian origin
doing excellent work when they find opportunities elsewhere. With
proper facilities, serious investment in education, and genuin
cooperation among stakeholders, more of that capacity can b
developed and applied at home.
4. For students who want to contribute to Nigeria’s technologica
development but have limited resources, where should they
begin?
Students should learn to recognise the commercial potential of thei
knowledge. Entrepreneurship has been introduced into the curriculum
for a reason: students should consider how an idea can become
product or service that people need.
Funding is a major challenge. Grants and scholarships are not alway
available, and a student may win a prize at an exhibition withou
receiving the sustained support needed to develop an idea further. I
students can gradually commercialise some of their skills, earn income
and build a business, they may be able to fund parts of their project
themselves.
My advice is to look inward and think about how to begin developin
an idea with the resources available. Keep working on it, seek suppor
where possible, and be persistent. Recognition and interest from
potential users or customers may open further opportunities. I
necessary, a student may take up another business to raise money and
later return to the project.
The important thing is not to abandon an idea simply because the firs
attempt to find funding fails. We need stronger institutions that can
help promising ideas develop, but students should also keep learning
build their capacity, and pursue their ideas with determination.
5. If you could leave the graduating class with one principle to
guide their careers, what would it be?
I would tell them to uphold professional ethics: transparency
accountability, and responsibility. Wherever you work as an engineer
be open and sincere, take responsibility for your actions, and be ready
to account for the work entrusted to you. These qualities help peopl
trust you and the work you do.
Responsibility also shows in everyday conduct. When lecturers insis
that students attend class on time, they are not only teaching cours
content; they are also encouraging punctuality and responsibility. I
you cannot attend, be honest about the reason. Sincerity matters. Th
habits you develop as a student can follow you into the workplace
where you may eventually lead a team or be responsible for a project.
So my advice to the graduating class is to be transparent, accountable
and responsible. Take your work seriously, be sincere with people, and
do not take your duties for granted. These qualities will help other
have confidence in you and your professional judgement.
Engr. A. I. Dalyop

![[../images/interview_dalyop.jpg]]

---

title: Interview — Bridging the Theory and Practice
rawContent:
# Interview — Bridging the Theory and Practice

Dr. K. O. Lawal — Chairman, NIEEEE Bauchi
An electrical engineering educator on modern curricula,
industry collaboration, and practical solutions for Nigeria
“Identify a problem in your environment, then use what you
have learned to tackle it.”
Q1. What do students often misunderstand about
electrical engineering before they appreciate its practical
applications?
Electrical engineering depends on a strong understanding of
its fundamental concepts. Students need to build that
foundation from the beginning, regardless of their level. The
relevant equations explain the processes and phenomena
they study. Once students understand the concepts and
equations, they can better appreciate how the knowledge is
applied in real situations.
Q2. Universities often emphasise theory, while graduates
are expected to solve practical problems. Where is the
gap most evident, and how can it be addressed?
The curriculum needs regular updating so that it reflects
changes in technology. A university of technology should
provide a proper blend of theory and practical work, with
greater attention to skills. Some subjects require students to
work directly with equipment and develop hands-on
understanding. In my own classes, I have introduced concepts
beyond the formal curriculum when I felt some content had
become outdated. Students need to leave university able to
combine what they know with what they can do.
Q3. As chairman of the Bauchi State branch of the
engineering institute, what role should the institute play
in connecting education, professional practice, and
society?
The institute has organised training opportunities for
students and worked to strengthen links between
universities and industry. I have visited organisations
including TCN, JED, and the Ministry of Power to explore how
industry challenges might be connected with university
expertise. Where a problem can be addressed through
research or technical support, the university and industry can
work together. We have also organised training for students,
although students must be willing to take advantage of those
opportunities.

Q4. Nigeria continues to face electricity-supply and
energy-infrastructure challenges. Which issues need
more attention, and how can engineers help?
A major concern is that much of the power infrastructure is
old and needs modernisation, particularly the transmission
network. If the network cannot carry the power being
generated, the country cannot make full use of its generation
capacity. Modern technologies, including smart-grid systems,
can also help detect faults more quickly. Nigeria has energy
resources such as hydro and solar power; upgrading the
network and ensuring that people have the expertise to
operate modern systems would help the country make
better use of them.
Q5. Many engineering projects do not move beyond the
university. What would help research become practical
solutions to Nigeria’s challenges?
I encourage students I supervise to look at their own
environment and identify problems their projects could
solve. Students sometimes focus only on finishing their
degrees quickly, even though there are many real-world
challenges that technology can address. Last year, we
converted a fuel-powered motorcycle into an electric
motorcycle, and I have used it on campus. It is one example
of how engineering can respond to mobility challenges and
rising fuel costs. Students should identify a problem, apply
what they have learned, and make an attempt—even if the
first result is not perfect.
Q6. What technical skills, professional habits, and sense
of responsibility should graduating students develop as
they enter professional practice?
Students need to recognise and close the gap between their
university training and the skills expected in the workplace.
That is why workshops and induction activities are
important. We have organised training on topics such as
solar installation and soft skills to help final-year students
prepare for current professional demands. My advice is to
keep doing what can be done to support students’
development and to encourage them to take these
opportunities seriously.
Dr. K. O. Lawal

![[../images/interview_lawal.jpg]]

title: Interview — Engineering with Purpose: Start Solving the Problems Around You
rawContent:
# Interview — Engineering with Purpose: Start Solving the Problems Around You

th e Pro blem s Aro u n d Y o u
Engr. Ruqayya Aliyu Tilde
From choosing Engineering out of genuine passion to
encouraging students to build solutions around local needs…
“Solve your national issues that will attract international
attention.”
From being an engineering student to becoming a member of
academic staff, what experience has shaped you the most?
One of the things that helped me most at university was allowing the
experience to shape me. University is not only about reading for
examinations and earning good grades; it is also about building
relationships, making connections, working hard, and discovering what you
want to do with your life.
I often tell students that whatever they do should have a purpose. Do not
pursue a degree simply for the sake of having one. I remember that, when I
was in secondary school, many of my classmates wanted to study medicine,
while only a few of us applied for engineering. I loved engineering and was
good at mathematics, so my father suggested that I study mathematics. He
even changed my course to Mathematics when we came to the university,
but I told him that engineering was my passion.
That commitment helped me stay on my chosen path. After graduation, I
got married and had children, so I had to balance family responsibilities
with pursuing my ambitions. Building good relationships with my lecturers
as an undergraduate also shaped how I relate to people in the department
today. It feels like being at home. I always encourage young people to work
hard and to do things with purpose. When you genuinely love what you do,
that passion helps sustain you.
What do students most often overlook about becoming competent
engineers?
I think a major challenge is a lack of passion. Some students want
everything to be easy, and that can affect how deeply they engage with
their studies. However, we should not blame students entirely. Economic
pressures also affect them. Some students are trying to study while
worrying about feeding themselves, paying fees, and what will happen after
school.
When people lack financial security, they can become preoccupied with
immediate survival rather than having the space to think creatively. So the
issue is both individual and societal. Students need to find purpose in what
they are doing, but we must also recognise the pressures that make
learning difficult. Not everyone has to follow the same path or obtain a
degree to succeed; people have different strengths and talents.
Understanding your purpose can help you choose a path that fits you and
commit to it.
As a woman working in a field where women are underrepresented,
what has your experience been like?
My undergraduate years helped me build good relationships with my
lecturers, so returning to the department as a member of staff did not feel
like entering a strange environment. It felt as though I was returning to a
family I already knew. Because of that, I cannot fully relate to some of the
difficulties people describe when working in a male-dominated
environment; my own experience has been shaped by those existing
relationships.
Wherever you find yourself, build good relationships and do what is right.
Stay away from practices such as bribery and other forms of misconduct.
Relationships, integrity, and emotional intelligence matter alongside
technical ability. Intelligence alone cannot take you everywhere if you
cannot work with people. We are social beings, and we need one another to
succeed.
What discourages some young women from pursuing engineering, and
what can universities do to address this?
Society plays a major role. In conservative communities, some people still
expect women to focus only on the home and may not recognise that a
woman can be productive professionally and also be a good wife or mother.
We need examples that show younger women that they, too, can pursue
engineering and other demanding careers.

At the same time, we should not assume that progress requires
copying every aspect of Western society. We can adapt educational and
professional systems in ways that fit our context and make women
more comfortable in engineering while preserving values that matter
to us. Another barrier is that some girls are made to believe that
mathematics, physics, and the sciences are too difficult. They should be
encouraged and supported to see that these subjects are learnable and
that they can succeed in them.
Universities can help by creating supportive environments, making
space for women’s participation, and providing visible role models
who demonstrate what is possible.
Nigeria faces major challenges in energy infrastructure and
technological development. Where can electrical and electronics
engineers make the most meaningful contribution?
Electrical engineering touches many fields, so there are opportunities
in several areas. We should look closely at the problems people are
experiencing now and develop solutions that respond to them. For
example, with the cost pressures associated with fuel and transport,
engineers could explore electric vehicles and alternative energy
options, including biogas-based solutions, where they are technically
and economically suitable.
Our challenges are complex, and each sector deserves serious
attention. A useful starting point is to understand the current economic
situation, identify a real need, and work towards a practical solution.
Engineers should not design in isolation from the circumstances of the
people who will use their work.
What do you wish you had understood about engineering earlier
in your career, and what advice would you give the graduating
class?
I wish I had simplified engineering by focusing more on the problems
around me. We do not always need to look at what another country has
done and assume its solution will fit our circumstances. Our problems
are often specific to our communities and country.
My advice to graduating students is to pay attention to local problems
and to what is happening in the market. You do not have to make an
impact internationally from the beginning. Solve national problems in
ways that can eventually attract international attention. Nigeria has a
large population and a substantial market for useful products and
services, so there is room for home-grown solutions to grow.
For example, there are opportunities to improve local agricultural and
poultry supply chains, including the availability of day-old chicks.
Engineers can observe such gaps and ask how design, technology, and
better processes might help address them. They should also examine
the reliability and quality of locally made equipment, such as egg
incubators, and work to improve performance. The same principle
applies to electronic components and other products: if we do not
develop and improve our own solutions, we may remain dependent on
products from elsewhere.
Be current with what is happening around you. Identify a need,
understand the gap, and work to fill it. Start with local problems, build
solutions that work, and allow those solutions to grow. Engineering
should make life easier for people.
A message to the graduating class
As the conversation concluded, Engr. Ruqayya Aliyu Tilde wished the
graduating students success and offered her continued support,
encouraging them to reach out when they need guidance. Her message
is a reminder that a meaningful engineering career is built23 not only on
technical knowledge, but also on purpose, integrity, relationships, and
a commitment to solving real problems.
Dr. R. A. Tilde

![[../images/interview_ruqayya.jpg]]

---
*Source: interview_section.pdf, page 10.*

title: Interview — Mentorship, Discipline and the Making of Responsible Engineers
rawContent:
# Interview — Mentorship, Discipline and the Making of Responsible Engineers

Meet Dr. A. A. Sadiq — PGD Coordinator
… reflects on student guidance, professional standards, and the
value of teamwork.
“Wherever you find yourself, try to be hardworking. Try to be a
team player. Don’t isolate yourself.”
1. Could you briefly introduce yourself and describe your area of
specialisation?
I am a lecturer in the Department of Electrical and Electronics
Engineering at ATBU. My area of specialisation is electronics,
particularly biomedical electronics and bioelectronics. At
undergraduate level, I teach courses that include Electrical
Engineering Fundamentals, Microwave Engineering and Reliability
Engineering, among others. I joined ATBU in 2008 as a Graduate
Assistant and have since progressed to the rank of Reader (Associate
Professor).
2. Beyond teaching, what do you consider your responsibility
towards the personal and professional development of students?
Teaching is only one part of the responsibility. Mentorship is also
important. I try to build a cordial relationship with my students,
especially those I supervise for their projects. That relationship often
goes beyond the project itself. We advise and guide students
whenever they need support, whether the matter concerns their
academics or aspects of their personal lives. Our responsibility is to
mentor them and help them make informed decisions.
3. There appears to be a mentorship gap in the Department. How
do you think it can be addressed?
I agree that there is a gap. The Department has level coordinators
who are expected to maintain direct contact with students and
provide a point of support when they need advice or are facing
difficulties. However, the growing student population has increased
the workload on lecturers, and this arrangement has not worked as
effectively as it should. Students are often assisted when they
approach lecturers and explain their situations, but sometimes
lecturers may not know that a student is experiencing a problem. The
Department is therefore working on improving the mentorship
structure around the level-coordinator system.
4. Engineering mistakes can have serious consequences. How does
this reality influence the standards you expect students to
maintain during their training?
We expect students to follow the proper procedures and do the right
things at the right time. The recent project exhibition showed the
importance we place on maintaining standards. Students should be
able to design their projects, implement their designs and construct
their work properly. We do not want them to compromise quality.
Engineering requires care, discipline and a commitment to doing
things correctly.

5. What do students sometimes misunderstand abou
lecturers who insist on discipline and high standards?
Some students may see lecturers who insist on standards a
being wicked or unconcerned about their progress. In reality
the intention is to protect their education and future careers
Sometimes students are attracted to shortcuts, while lecturer
want them to put in the necessary effort and do the work
properly. Lecturers have also been students; we understand the
challenges because we have experienced them ourselves. We
want students to succeed, even when they may not immediately
understand why certain requirements are necessary.
6. What makes you feel that you have succeeded in you
responsibility towards the students you have taught?
Teaching itself is meaningful because we cannot always know
how far the knowledge shared in a classroom will travel. Afte
graduation, students may go on to make contributions to thei
communities, regions or the country. We have seen graduate
secure employment and others return to support the
University. Seeing former students progress and give back i
one of the things that makes me feel that I have made a
worthwhile contribution.
7. What final advice would you give to graduating students?
Wherever you find yourself, be hardworking and be a team
player. Do not isolate yourself. You have spent several year
with your classmates, and it is important to maintain thos
relationships after graduation. Build a network and stay
connected; social media platforms make it easier to keep in
touch, share opportunities and recommend one another
Teamwork is important, but self-discipline must come first
Wherever you go, strive to make a positive contribution.
Dr. A. A. Sadiq

![[../images/interview_sadiq.jpg]]

title: Interview — Think Beyond the Classroom
rawContent:
# Interview — Think Beyond the Classroom

Meet Dr. S. M. Yarima — Registration Officer
Building solutions, not just Careers…
“I want to measure my development based on how much I try to
develop the students themselves.”
1. Could you briefly introduce yourself and your areas of interest?
My name is Said Musa Yarima, and I am a lecturer in the Department of
Electrical and Electronics Engineering at ATBU. I teach courses in
communications and digital signal processing (DSP), as well as some
areas of mechatronics and embedded artificial intelligence. These are
among my particular areas of interest. I completed my primary and
secondary education in Bauchi, and then studied at ATBU for both my
undergraduate and master’s degrees. I obtained my PhD from
Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM) before returning to continue my
work in the Department.
2. Beyond teaching engineering, what do you consider your
responsibility towards the personal and professional development
of your students?
Different lecturers have different approaches, but my personal goal is
to see students progress to higher levels. I do not measure my
development mainly by personal gain; I measure it by how much I
contribute to the development of students. That is also why I have
taught outside the University. For about ten years, I volunteered to
teach at a local primary school, Kobe Primary School, and I have seen
some of those pupils grow into teachers and professionals. Some have
gone on to study fields such as medicine, while others have pursued
different careers. It is rewarding to meet former pupils years later and
see how far they have come.
I also want students to think beyond the immediate subject they are
studying. They should be able to connect what they learn in class with
other areas of life, including finance, economics and creativity. I have
taught programming, for example, and have seen students use what
they learned to develop practical projects and pursue opportunities in
different parts of the world. My aspiration is to see students become
independent thinkers and people of exemplary character.
3. There seems to be a mentorship gap in the Department. What do
you think contributes to it, and how can it be addressed?
I think the challenges come from several directions: students, lecturers
and the wider education system. Some students arrive at university
with weak foundations from their earlier schooling, making it difficult
for lecturers to bring everyone to the required level. Lecturers also
need to understand students’ circumstances rather than becoming
discouraged when some struggle to keep up.
There are practical limitations too. Students need opportunities to use
the tools and equipment they are taught about. For example, teaching
software such as MATLAB, Simulink and related engineering tools is
not enough if students never get the opportunity to practise with them.
They need to see and use these tools for themselves.
Economic pressures also affect students. Some have to support
themselves and pay their own expenses, which can make it difficult to
give their studies the same attention as students with greater financial
support. The wider society also influences students’ motivation and
expectations. Lecturers should therefore look beyond course content,
take time to understand students’ circumstances and ask why some are
struggling or losing interest. A more thoughtful understanding of
students’ needs can help lecturers find better ways to teach and mentor
them.

4. Students often know you through your lectures, but may no
know what informs your approach to teaching and interacting
with them. What would you like them to understand?
I try to use the time I have with students, even if it is only a few
minutes, to discuss their progress and the kind of positiv
contribution they can make in life. I want them to think about wha
they will be remembered for and how their actions can benefi
others.
Much of what I read is outside engineering. I am interested in
psychology, history, religion and social and political issues becaus
these subjects help me understand people and society. When
interact with students, I try to put myself in their position and
consider what they may be experiencing. I was the eldest child in a
family with limited means, so I understand something about th
pressure of having to work hard and overcome difficulties
Ultimately, students should look up to people because of good
qualities and positive contributions, not simply because of statu
or popularity.
5. What final advice would you give to the graduating class?
First, understand your environment and recognise th
opportunities around you. Nigeria has considerable natural and
human resources, and Nigerians have demonstrated their abilitie
in many parts of the world. Graduates should ask themselves how
they can use their knowledge and abilities to contribute at home.
During the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) year, do not spend
all your earnings without a plan. Consider forming a group with
trusted colleagues, pooling resources and exploring practica
business opportunities. You could seek guidance from institution
such as the Bank of Industry, build relationships with companies
and study areas where local needs are not being met. Agriculture
preservation and other essential services may offer opportunities
depending on what you understand and can manage.
An engineering graduate should not assume that useful work i
limited to the engineering sector. Skills from electrical engineerin
may also be applied in other industries. The example I gave was th
possibility of exploring locally needed pharmaceutical supplies and
hospital consumables. The important thing is to research the need
carefully, work with people who have the right expertise, and
develop a realistic plan. Do not wait only for a government job. B
disciplined, think creatively, start with the resources available to
you and focus on building a sustainable future before prioritisin
luxury or immediate enjoyment.
Dr. S. M. Yarima

title: Interview — The Value of a Strong Foundation
rawContent:
# Interview — The Value of a Strong Foundation

Meet Engr. A. A. SALIHU — Senior Lecturer
Engr. A. A. Salihu on practical engineering, discipline, integrity,
and preparing students for life beyond university…
“Any foundation built on falsehood will eventually crumble.”
1. Could you briefly introduce yourself and tell us about your
educational journey?
My name is Engr. A. A. Salihu. I was born in Sokoto in the early 1960s
and attended primary school in Jos. After spending a few years at an
Islamiyya school, I returned to Sokoto and continued my education at
a government secondary technical school in what was then Sokoto
State, an area now in Zamfara State. I later gained admission to ATBU,
where I was among the university’s early student cohorts. I graduated
with a Second Class Upper degree and was the best-performing
student in my set. After national service in Rivers State, including
service at an NNPC zonal office, I returned to ATBU and was appointed
a Graduate Assistant. I later completed my master’s degree. Around
1999 to 2001, I also served in Sierra Leone as a technical aid worker,
teaching at two institutions.
2. How has engineering education at ATBU changed since your
early days?
A great deal has changed, and some of those changes reflect wider
challenges in Nigeria. In the early days, ATBU graduates were known
for their practical ability. Many secured opportunities because of what
they could do with their hands, not simply because they held a
certificate. Students often demonstrated strong technical skills during
industrial training. Today, however, practical learning is more difficult
to deliver. Student numbers have grown significantly, laboratory
groups are much larger, and some equipment has become obsolete.
Course content also needs to keep pace with developments in the
wider world. Students still excel when they commit themselves, but
the university needs suitable equipment, updated teaching content,
and better conditions for practical work.
3. Beyond teaching engineering, what responsibility do you have
for students’ personal and professional development?
Lecturers should help students understand the realities of life and
work beyond the university. In the past, we were able to take some
students to small companies and industries so they could see how
classroom knowledge was applied in practice. Those experiences
helped connect theory with real working conditions. Today, the cost of
such activities and the decline of some small industries make this
harder. Even so, preparing students for life outside the university
remains an important part of our responsibility.
4. Why are discipline and competence especially important in
engineering?
People’s lives can depend on engineering decisions, and a single
serious mistake can have grave consequences. Students therefore
need a sound understanding of their field, its rules, and its
professional standards. They also need guidance from experienced
people as they develop. We must not allow students to pass without
gaining the knowledge and practical competence required of them.
For example, when students skip classes or laboratory sessions but
rely on classmates to complete work or record attendance for them,
they are not being helped. They are being put at risk, and they may
eventually put others at risk too. Staff and students must work
together to protect the standards of the profession.

5. Why are lecturers who insist on high standard
sometimes seen as difficult or unapproachable?
Some students form an opinion about a lecturer before they
have even met the person, often because of what others hav
told them. When a lecturer refuses to tolerate shortcuts o
dishonesty, students may interpret that as being difficult. Bu
maintaining standards is not the same as being
unapproachable. If a student has a genuine problem, I expec
them to come and explain it so we can discuss a solution
Writing tests for other students or falsifying attendance may
look like helping a friend, but it does not prepare that person
for professional responsibility.
6. How can lecturers understand students’ circumstance
while still holding them accountable?
A student’s values and habits are shaped long before university
beginning in primary and secondary school. Universities can
guide and support students, but changing established habit
may take considerable effort. In earlier years, lecturers could
know students individually, understand their strengths and
weaknesses, and provide more personal guidance. Large classe
make that much harder. Students also face distractions
including spending excessive time on their phones. At the same
time, the internet offers valuable learning resources if they us
it well. We need to guide students, understand their challenge
where possible, and still expect them to take responsibility fo
their education.
7. What do you hope students will understand about your
teaching approach when they look back?
My guiding principle is that whatever knowledge God gives you
you should pass it on rather than hold it back. I believe I wil
one day be accountable for my actions, and that belie
influences how I teach. Some students may not appreciate stric
standards while they are still in school, but later, when they face
the demands of working life or continue to postgraduate study
they often understand why those standards mattered. When
students are truthful and willing to follow the rules, they can
have a good relationship with me. The problem arises when
people expect to cut corners.
8. What gives you the greatest satisfaction as an educator?
I feel happy when I see students who passed through me
succeed after graduation. Many have returned to expres
appreciation, including those who went on to postgraduat
studies. Some former students have told their own children to
take their work seriously because they remember the value o
the training they received. Knowing that what I taught them ha
remained useful in their lives is a great source of joy.
What is your advice to graduating students?
Set a goal for yourself. You may not achieve every goal you set
but it is a mistake to move through life without having one. Do
your best and trust Allah to guide your path. Remember you
parents and appreciate the sacrifices they made to bring you
this far. Be kind to your family, neighbours, and others who may
depend on your help. Above all, be truthful. Do not take wha
belongs to others or misuse money entrusted to you. Th
younger generation will eventually take responsibility for the
country, and Nigeria’s future depends on the integrity and
character you build today. I wish all graduating student
success in their future endeavours.
Engr. A. A. Salihu

![[../images/interview_salihu.jpg]]

---
