title: Interview — The Teacher Behind the Engineer
rawContent:
# Interview — The Teacher Behind the Engineer

Meet Dr. Sani Sabo — Project Coordinator
A conversation on mentorship, practical skills, and the human
side of engineering education
“Students should not be afraid of their lecturers. They should
come close to them, so that lecturers can guide and support
them.”
1. Could you briefly introduce yourself?
My name is Muhammad Sani Sabo, and I am from Toro Local
Government Area of Bauchi State. I attended primary and
secondary school before gaining admission to Abubakar Tafawa
Balewa University, where I studied Electrical Engineering. After
graduating, I was appointed as a Graduate Assistant, and that
marked the beginning of my career as an academic and lecturer
in the department.
2. What do students need most from their lecturers beyond
classroom teaching?
Students should not be guided by rumours that some lecturers
are friendly while others are harsh. They should approach all
their lecturers and ask questions whenever they have difficulties.
They should also know their level adviser, who can guide them
on university rules, regulations, and the steps they need to take
to graduate successfully. Students should not be afraid of their
lecturers; they should feel comfortable approaching them for
guidance and counselling.
3. What gives you the greatest satisfaction when teaching?
I feel fulfilled when I teach a class and can see that many of the
students understand the lesson and are encouraged by what
they have learned. It gives me joy to know that I have
contributed something useful to them—something they can
remember and apply wherever they find themselves.
4. What separates students who understand engineering
from those who study mainly to pass examinations?
Students need to understand why they are in school and what
will be expected of them in the labour market. Engineering
requires skills, so practical experience is essential. Students
should not rely only on memorising information for
examinations. Even when every practical skill cannot be fully
covered in class, they should seek additional training and
opportunities to build their competence.
5. Many students describe you as one of their favourite
lecturers. Why do you think that is?
I consider all lecturers important. I see the students I meet as
younger brothers and sisters, and I try to bring them close, tell
them the truth, and show them ways to overcome difficulties
without becoming discouraged. I believe that this supportive
approach may be why some students regard me as a favourite
lecturer.
6. How do you balance being approachable with
maintaining authority and discipline?
I have never wanted to make students feel that they can only
approach me in my office. I tell them they can ask questions
wherever they meet me, even in the canteen. If a question needs
a fuller explanation, we can go to a classroom or office and use a
board or other materials to work through it. I believe helping a
student should come before formality.

7. What do you consider the greatest challenges facing
university education in Nigeria?
For a technological institution, equipment is very important
because students need practical training. Lecturers also need a
conducive working environment, including teaching materials,
internet access, suitable offices, and the resources required to
demonstrate concepts. Staff motivation and fair remuneration
matter too. In addition, admission bodies and schools should
work together to ensure that students enter university with
sound foundational knowledge. Weak preparation makes it
much harder for lecturers to build advanced understanding.
8. What has teaching taught you about patience, discipline,
and human potential?
Teaching requires commitment and patience because students
have different personalities and learn in different ways.
Lecturers should correct students without being unnecessarily
harsh, and should treat them with care while still showing them
the right path. Teachers also need to keep improving
themselves so that their knowledge and abilities continue to
grow.
9. What do you hope students will remember about you
after they have forgotten the details of your courses?
I hope they remember the human side of our interactions. I
sometimes use humour and give students nicknames, which can
make a class more lively and help students remember those
moments. I also try to apologise if I say something that hurts a
student. Beyond the subject matter, I hope they remember the
encouragement and the moments of laughter we shared.
10. When you think about former students, what matters
more: the engineers they become or the people they
become along the way?
It gives me great joy to meet former students during
professional assignments, especially when I visit tertiary
institutions. I am pleased to see them working and contributing.
I also think about the generations that will come after them,
including my own children and grandchildren, and I hope they
will benefit from the work and character of the people I have
taught.
11. What improvements would you like to see in the
Department of Electrical Engineering?
The department should strengthen students’ practical
experience by providing more components and opportunities
for hands-on learning. Although laboratory work is already
carried out, practical project skills should be reinforced at
higher levels, including 400 and 500 levels, so students are
better prepared for the work they will face after graduation. I
would also like to see a closer, more supportive relationship
between lecturers and students. When students feel welcomed
and supported, they are more likely to be happy, engaged, and
ready to learn.
Dr. Sani Sabo

title: EXAMINATION COUNTDOWN TIMER MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
rawContent:
# EXAMINATION COUNTDOWN TIMER MANAGEMENT SYSTEM

**Student(s):** Abdulhyyu Muhd, Levi Dashe, Idris A. Shuaib, Caeb Ponsak Philip, Sani Philip Friday, Abdulgafar Saliu  
**Supervisor:** Engr. Yusuf Saleh

![[../images/project_examination_countdown_timer.jpg]]

## ABSTRACT

Examination candidates need to know at every moment how much time remains, yet wall clocks, announcements and times written on a board are hard to read in a large hall and cannot track several papers of different durations. Simple electronic timers also lose their count when power fails. This project aimed to design and construct a microcontroller-based examination countdown time management system that displays up to three courses at once and keeps correct time through power interruptions. The system uses two ATmega328P microcontrollers linked by a 9600-baud UART connection protected by a CRC-8 check. The master controller handles a 4 × 4 matrix keypad, a DS1307 real-time clock (RTC), a buzzer and the top display row, while the slave drives the bottom row. The display is a 192 × 32 pixel board of twelve two-colour P10 LED modules in two rows of six, with course names on the red row and countdown times on the green row.

title: GAS LEAKAGE DETECTOR WITH ALARM SYSEM & FIRE FIGHTING CAPABILITY
rawContent:
# GAS LEAKAGE DETECTOR WITH ALARM SYSEM & FIRE FIGHTING CAPABILITY

**Student(s):** Abdulliadi Abdulbaki, Yahaya Tajudeedn A., Yusuf Hikmat O.  
**Supervisor:** Dr. H. S. Miya

![[../images/project_gas_leakage_detector.jpg]]

## ABSTRACT

The increasing cases of Fire outbreaks and gas leakage in Nigerian homes and commercial buildings have created a need for affordable and reliable safety systems. Many existing systems have limitations, such as the use of single sensors, lack of remote alerts, and absence of automatic fire response. This project focuses on the design and construction of a Smart Gas Leakage Detector with Fire Fighting Capability to help address these problems.

The system is built around the ATmega328P microcontroller. It uses three gas sensors (MQ-2, MQ-5, and MQ-6) to detect combustible gases in the environment. When gas is detected above the set limit, the system activates a buzzer and sends an SMS alert to a registered phone number through the SIM800L GSM module.

rawContent:
# DESIGN AND CONSTRUCTION OF AN AUTONOMOUS OBSTACLE-AVOIDING WHEELED ROBOT

**Student(s):** Abdulazeez Suleimn  
**Supervisor:** Engr. Abdulrazak Sabo

![[../images/project_obstacle_avoiding_robot.jpg]]

## ABSTRACT

This project involves the design and construction of an autonomous wheeled robot capable of detecting and avoiding obstacles without human assistance. Using an ultrasonic sensor, the robot detects objects within a preset distance of 20 cm and automatically reverses and changes direction to prevent collisions. The system demonstrates the practical application of robotics and automation in areas such as industrial operations, healthcare delivery, and smart transportation.

It is with joy and gratitude that I congratulate the 43rd EEE Balewite Dynamos on reaching the end of this journey.

As we leave ATBU for new roads, I wish every Dynamo good health, success and good character. Wherever we go, let us carry this department's name with pride and keep the bonds we built here.

Congratulations, Dynamos.
